newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives hit by new sleaze resignation.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives hit by new sleaze resignation.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservative Party, already fighting an uphill battle against sleaze allegations before May 1 national elections, was dealt a body blow on Saturday when its Scottish election chief resigned, citing a "personal indiscretion".
Sir Michael Hirst, chairman of the Conservative Party in Scotland, said in a letter to Prime Minister John Major that he was resigning rather than embarrass the party.
"I very deeply regret these circumstances which have caused great distress to my family and which may, I fear, cause embarrassment to the party in the current climate," he said in a letter.

Hirst was the third senior Conservative to resign his post in a week dominated by sexual and money scandals and thwarted attempts by the Conservatives to dent the opposition Labour Party's 25 point lead in opinion polls.
Allan Stewart resigned his position as Conservative MP in the safest seat in Scotland on Monday after reports linking him to a married woman and a clinic for alcoholics.
MP Tim Smith resigned on Wednesday over his role in a two-year long scandal about MPs who took cash from businessmen and lobbyists in return for asking questions in parliament.

Neil Hamilton is also under pressure to quit over the cash for questions scandal and a fifth man -- MP Piers Merchant -- has been told to explain himself after newspaper reports that he had an affair with a 17-year-old nightclub hostess.

Hirst gave no indication of the nature of his "indiscretion" but said he was "desolated" to have failed Major just five weeks before polling day. He dropped his bombshell as Major took time off the campaign to mark his 54th birthday at the Oval cricket ground.
Hirst is the latest casualty of Major's short-lived "back to basics" moral crusade that quickly backfired in 1993 and has caused the resignation of more than 16 Conservative ministers or aides.
Annabel Goldie, who has replaced Hirst as Scottish party chairman, dismissed suggestions that the latest scandal would worsen the Conservatives' election chances.
She told Britain's Sky News that voters were more concerned about the economy, health and education than personal morality.
"I am absolutely satisfied that as voters approach polling day they're going to focus on, and be solely concerned with, the issues that affect them.

"I think the public is beginning to feel it has had enough, that it is beginning to resent the attempt by the media to judge...to devastate and destroy the lives of people who in many respects are good, upright and honourable people who have merely done what many others have done -- made a mistake," Goldie said.

Labour, trying to end 18 years of Conservative rule, on Saturday stepped up the pressure on Hamilton to resign. Its candidate in Hamilton's staunchly Conservative Tatton constituency in central England said he was prepared to step aside in favour of a non-political "anti-corruption" candidate.
Labour acknowledged that the move was designed to shame Hamilton into standing down. The Conservatives described it as an election gimmick in a seat that Labour never stood a chance of winning.
